items.title: fix(server): keep the Node adapters running when a streamed body fails or errorFormatter throws
items.body:
🤖 ## Why - With the standalone, Express and Next.js adapters, a streamed body that fails after its headers were sent made `internal_exceptionHandler` write a second response. Node then threw an uncaught `write after end`, and the process exited. One cause is a JSONL value that `JSON.stringify` can't handle, such as a `bigint`. - A throwing `errorFormatter` made the same handler throw. The request got no response, and the rejection was unhandled. ## What - `internal_exceptionHandler` only ends a response whose headers were already sent. - If the error formatter throws, it answers with a minimal `INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR` that reveals nothing about the error, like the ws adapter since #7915. ## Links None ## Alternatives considered - Make a JSONL value that can't be serialized fail only its own call. That's a bigger change to the stream producer, so it goes into the `resolveResponse` rewrite (#7894) instead. ## Testing Regression check: both tests in `nodeHTTPExceptionHandler.test.ts` fail on `main`. The first records the uncaught `write after end`. The second never gets a response. ## AI model Claude Opus 5.5

items.title: fix(server): respect maxBodySize in the Fastify adapter
items.body:
## Why - The Fastify adapter always passed `maxBodySize: null` to `incomingMessageToRequest`, so there was no way to cap request bodies the way the Standalone and Express adapters can. - Fastify hands `multipart/form-data` bodies to tRPC as the raw request stream. `createBody` forwarded that stream as is, so even a set limit never applied to it. ## What - `FastifyHandlerOptions` gets `maxBodySize?: number`, and `fastifyRequestHandler` passes it through (`opts.maxBodySize ?? null`). - `createBody` now reads a raw `IncomingMessage` handed over as `req.body` through the same size-checked stream as an unparsed request, so a larger body gets `413 PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE`. - JSON bodies are still read by Fastify, so they stay capped by Fastify's `bodyLimit` (1 MiB by default). items.title: fix(server): enforce maxBatchSize for WebSocket batches
items.body:
## Why - `maxBatchSize` is part of the options every handler takes, and the WebSocket handler's types accept it. But `applyWSSHandler` and `getWSConnectionHandler` ignore it, so a WebSocket message holding a JSON array of any length runs every request in it. - On HTTP, an oversized batch gets a `400 BAD_REQUEST` (`Batch call exceeds maximum size`) and no procedure runs. The WebSocket handler should behave the same. ## What - `packages/server/src/adapters/ws.ts`: when a message is an array longer than `maxBatchSize`, reject the whole batch: - It checks the length right after decoding and before `parseTRPCMessage`, so no input is deserialized and no procedure runs. - It calls `onError` once, the same way HTTP does: `type: 'unknown'`, no `path` or `input`, `BAD_REQUEST`, `Batch call exceeds maximum size`. - It sends that error to every request id in the batch (echoing `jsonrpc`), so `wsLink` calls reject like `httpBatchLink` calls do instead of waiting forever. `subscription.stop` entries get no reply, as before. If no entry has a usable id, it sends one `id: null` error. - It reads the existing `maxBatchSize` option on the handler options (from `BaseHandlerOptions`). No new API. With Fastify `useWSS`, the same `trpcOptions.maxBatchSize` now applies to both HTTP and WebSocket. - Docs: a short "Limiting batch size" section on the WebSockets page (`www/v11/docs/server/websockets.md`). ```ts applyWSSHandler({ wss, router, maxBatchSize: 10 }); // A WebSocket message with 11 requests now gets 11 BAD_REQUEST errors and runs nothing. ``` ## Links - Related: #7704 (WebSocket subscription lifecycle rewrite). See the merge-order note under Testing. ## Alternatives considered - **One `id: null` error for the whole message**, the same way WebSocket parse errors are sent. Closest to HTTP's single response, but `wsLink` drops messages with `id: null`, so every call in the batch would hang. - **Parse first, then check the size.** Simpler, but it deserializes every input of a batch we are about to reject. HTTP checks the size before reading inputs too. - **Close the connection.** Harsher than HTTP, and it would also kill unrelated subscriptions on the same socket. - **A WebSocket-only option name.** Not needed, because the handler options already include `maxBatchSize`. ## Testing - New `packages/tests/server/websockets.maxBatchSize.test.ts`: - A raw WebSocket batch over the limit gets, for each id, the same error `code`, `message`, `data.code` and `data.httpStatus` as an HTTP batch over the limit (checked against the HTTP response in the same test). No procedure runs, and `onError` is called once. - `wsLink` calls that end up in an oversized batch reject with `BAD_REQUEST`. - A batch within the limit runs. - Without `maxBatchSize`, a batch of 50 runs. - Regression check: the new test failed on unmodified `main` (2 of 4 failed). The oversized batch was not rejected (`expected { code: undefined, …(3) } to deeply equal { code: -32600, …(3) }`), and the `wsLink` calls were `fulfilled` instead of `rejected`. With the fix, all 4 pass. - `packages/tests/server` (88 files, 694 tests) passes, including the existing WebSocket tests and the HTTP `maxBatchSize` recipe in `standalone.test.ts`. `oxlint`, `oxfmt --check` and `tsc` pass for `packages/server` and `packages/tests`. - Merge order with #7704: the change stays inside the message-parsing block that #7704 doesn't edit. `git merge-tree` merges cleanly in both directions, and the merged tree passes the WebSocket and Fastify tests, including #7704's lifecycle tests. The two PRs can merge in either order with no rebase. ## AI model Claude Opus 5.5
  
--- Open in [code]smith · Need help on this PR? Tag @codesmith-bot with what you need. ## Summary by CodeRabbit - **New Features** - WebSocket servers can limit the number of requests in a batch. Oversized batches are rejected with a `BAD_REQUEST` error, and none of their procedures run. - Each eligible request in an oversized batch receives an error response; `subscription.stop` requests are excluded. Batches within the limit continue to work, and no limit applies unless one is configured. - **Documentation** - Added guidance on WebSocket batch limits, oversized-batch behavior, and how requests are grouped into batches.

items.title: docs: reject cross-origin WebSocket upgrades in docs and examples
items.body:
## Why - Browsers don't apply CORS to WebSockets. A page on any origin can open a WebSocket to your server, and the browser sends its cookies with it. - Apps that authenticate WebSocket connections with cookies should check the `Origin` header against an allowlist. The WebSockets page didn't say so or show how. ## What - New "Rejecting cross-origin connections" section on the WebSockets page, after "Limiting batch size". - Shows the callback form of `verifyClient` on `new WebSocketServer({ port, verifyClient })`, checking `origin` against an allowlist and answering `403` for an origin it doesn't trust, as the examples do. - Notes that non-browser clients may omit `Origin`, so the app decides whether to allow a missing one. - One sentence on the alternative for `noServer: true`: check `req.headers.origin` in the `upgrade` listener, and end the socket with a `403` response (`socket.end('HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden\r\n…')`) instead of calling `wss.handleUpgrade()`. - The 4 examples that run a WebSocket server now check `Origin` against an allowlist. `WS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS` (comma-separated, entries trimmed) replaces the default: - `standalone-server`: `http://localhost:2022`. Allows a missing `Origin`, because its Node client sends none. - `fastify-server`: `http://localhost:2022`. Allows a missing `Origin`, for the same reason. - `next-websockets-encoder`: `http://localhost:3000`. Rejects a missing `Origin`. - `next-prisma-websockets-starter`: `http://localhost:3000`. On Vercel, `https://` plus the current deployment's own `https://$VERCEL_URL`. Rejects a missing `Origin`. Its Vercel route `api/trpc-ws` answers `403` before upgrading. ## Links - Docs: [WebSockets](https://www-git-cursor-ws-origin-check-docs-3334-trpc.vercel.app/docs/server/websockets) - [Rejecting cross-origin connections](https://www-git-cursor-ws-origin-check-docs-3334-trpc.vercel.app/docs/server/websockets#rejecting-cross-origin-connections): new section. - WebSockets example: [Home](https://next-prisma-websockets-starter-git-cursor-ws-origin-630d56-trpc.vercel.app/): live messages still arrive over `/api/trpc-ws` from the preview's own origin. ## Alternatives considered - An origin allowlist option on `applyWSSHandler`: the adapter receives connections after `ws` has accepted the upgrade, so `ws` is the right place to refuse them, and it already has `verifyClient`. - Showing only the `upgrade` listener approach, which the `ws` README prefers: it needs more code (an HTTP server, `noServer: true`, `handleUpgrade`), so it gets one sentence and `verifyClient` gets the example. ## Testing - No new tests. The changes are docs and example code, and the examples' existing E2E tests cover the allowed path. - `pnpm check-twoslash` in `www`: all 465 Twoslash blocks compiled, including the new one against the installed `ws` and `@types/ws`. `pnpm --filter www build` passes, and so do the `www` tests (40 files, 328 tests). - Ran the snippet's logic against a real `ws` server with `applyWSSHandler`: an allowed origin connects and gets a query result, another origin gets HTTP 403, and a request with no `Origin` connects. - Ran the `noServer: true` + `socket.end(...)` variant against a real `ws` client: an allowed origin connects, and another origin gets `HTTP 403 Forbidden`. - Examples: ran `pnpm turbo --filter ./examples/` with `test-dev`, `build`, `typecheck` and `test-start`, as CI does. Also ran `lint` and `tsc --noEmit` in each, and `oxfmt --check` and `oxlint` on the changed files. All pass. - `standalone-server`, `fastify-server`: the Node clients still receive subscription data over WebSockets. - `next-prisma-websockets-starter`: Playwright `1 passed` on `test-dev` and on `test-start`, against a local Postgres. - `next-websockets-encoder`: `build` and `typecheck` pass. It has no tests. - Manual check with Node `ws` against the standalone, Fastify and encoder servers. A foreign `Origin` gets `403`, and an allowed `Origin` connects. A missing `Origin` connects to the Node-client examples and gets `403` from the encoder. With `WS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS='http://a.example, http://localhost:2022'`, both entries connect. The Prisma Vercel route's `GET()` returns `403` for a foreign or missing `Origin`. ## Known, out of scope - The Next examples' `prodServer.ts` attaches `ws` with `{ server }` and also calls `wss.handleUpgrade()` in its own `upgrade` listener. Before this change too, each accepted connection logs "handleUpgrade() was called more than once". Next.js catches it, and the socket stays open. `verifyClient` on the constructor runs on both paths, so the check holds. ## AI model Claude Opus 5.5

items.title: fix(server): settle pending next() on abort and ignore teardown emissions in observableToAsyncIterable
items.body:
## Why `observableToAsyncIterable` (in `@trpc/server/observable`) has two bugs that block reusing it for async-iterable client subscriptions (#7850): - Aborting `signal` never settles a pending `next()`, so a `for await` loop hangs. - When an observable calls `complete()` during teardown, as `httpSubscriptionLink` does, `break` throws `Controller is already closed`. ## What - The helper now works like Node's `events.on()`, with two queues instead of a `ReadableStream`. - Abort, completion or `return()` unsubscribes and resolves every pending `next()` with `{ done: true }`. Queued values come first, except after `return()`. - Emissions after the iterator finishes are ignored. A throwing teardown still ends every pending `next()`, and `return()` rejects with its error. - On abort, `next()` resolves rather than rejecting with an `AbortError`, so `adapters/ws.ts` doesn't report a stop the client asked for as an error. - No client or API changes. ## Links None ## Alternatives considered - #7461's `active` flag on `observableToReadableStream`: keeps the stream and all its states. - Reject with `AbortError`, as Node does: see the `ws.ts` race above. ## Testing `aborting ends a pending next()` and `completing during teardown does not throw on break` fail on `main` and pass here. ## AI model Claude Opus 5.5

Tag @codesmith-bot with what you need. ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Bug Fixes** * Improved async iteration behavior when a stream is aborted, completed, or encounters an error. Pending reads now resolve or reject appropriately, and later reads finish cleanly. * Queued values are delivered before a stored error or the end of iteration. * Breaking iteration now handles source completion during teardown, and `return()` resolves after the source completes. A teardown error rejects the call that ends iteration without leaving other pending reads unresolved.

items.title: ci: don't cancel in-progress main push runs
items.body: ## Why - Every push to `main` shared one concurrency group with `cancel-in-progress: true`. When the merge queue lands several PRs at once, a run queued later for an older commit can cancel the tip's run. - That turned 472e6ba red: [run 41881709178](https://github.com/trpc/trpc/actions/runs/41881709178), for its parent 6b2fa56, cancelled [run 41881657094](https://github.com/trpc/trpc/actions/runs/41881657094), for the tip. ## What - `main.yml` and `lint.yml`: a push to `main` gets its own group, keyed by SHA (`main-refs/heads/main-`). Release commits keep their own group. - Unchanged: PRs, `next`/`canary` pushes and merge queue runs. `subtree.yml`, `release.yml` and the scheduled jobs serialise on purpose. - Cost: every push to `main` runs to the end, and on `main` that's only the unit test job. ## Links None ## Alternatives considered - `cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.ref != 'refs/heads/main' }}`: with a shared group, a newly queued run still replaces the pending one. - Doing nothing: `main` goes red whenever the queue lands a batch out of order. ## Testing `actionlint` passes. After merge, check that the next `main` push runs use a `main-refs/heads/main-` group. ## AI model Claude Opus 5.5 --- Open in [code]smith · Need help on this PR? Tag @codesmith-bot with what you need. ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Chores** * Updated automation run grouping for pushes to the main branch. Runs are now distinguished by commit, while other pushes continue to be grouped by workflow and branch. This changes how overlapping automation runs are scheduled; it does not change any end-user-facing functionality.

items.title: fix(client): don't flush a later WebSocket request onto a connecting socket
items.body: ## Why - Each `wsClient` request starts its own flush run: wait for the socket, `sleep(0)`, then send the queue. After a batch fails because its socket closed, a leftover run can flush a new request onto the next socket while it's still connecting, and the request fails with `Active connection is not open`. - Found while working on #7910. Reproduces on `main` (472e6ba) alone, separate from #7727 and #7910. ## What - `batchSend`: after `sleep(0)`, if the socket isn't open and this run's own request was already sent, return without flushing. Each queued request's own run sends it once the new socket opens. - New `RequestManager.isOutgoing(message)` checks whether a message is still queued. - Batching on an open socket is unchanged. No public API or wire format changes. ## Links None ## Alternatives considered - Flush only when the run's own request is still queued: it changes batching on an open socket. - Return whenever the socket isn't open: in lazy mode, a batch whose socket closed during the sleep would hang. ## Testing Both tests in `websockets.flushAfterBatchFailure.test.ts` fail on `main` 472e6ba with `Active connection is not open` in 30/30 runs, and pass with the fix. ## AI model Claude Opus 5.5 --- Open in [code]smith · Need help on this PR? Tag @codesmith-bot with what you need. ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Bug Fixes** * Improved WebSocket request handling when a connection closes during a batch. Requests affected by the interruption now fail cleanly, while requests made after reconnection can proceed successfully. * Added coverage for connection failures and recovery across concurrent requests.

items.title: fix(v12): port the v11 WebSocket fixes (#7704, #7888, #7889, #7891, #7892, #7861) to v12 sockets and wsLink
items.body:
🤖 Brings v12's WebSocket handlers and `wsLink` up to date with the v11 WebSocket fixes that landed on `main` on Nov 3–4: #7704, #7888, #7889, #7891 and #7892, plus the #7861 docs. Each upstream PR is a separate commit, adapted to v12's code, with its regression tests. It also makes the v11 interop handler reply `stopped` to a subscription stopped before it starts (plan decision D5, option A), this PR's original change. v12's `v11/` folder gets the v11 code itself from the next merge of `main` into `v12`; this PR changes only `next/` and `www/v12/docs/`. ## Why v12 had the same bugs, in its own code: - A subscription's procedure that throws after a stop or a close (in its generator's `finally`, or a `return()` that rejects) went nowhere: no client hears it, and `onError` never got it. - After a stop during the procedure, the iterable the procedure returns late was never disposed. - A subscription whose iteration fails didn't abort `opts.signal`, so a cleanup that waits for it never finished. - `retryLink` resends a call with the same operation id, so frames still arriving for the failed attempt reached the retry. - A `connectionParams` that throws, or a WebSocket that doesn't open, failed calls with a bare "The connection was lost", dropping the error. A client that sent `subscription.stop` during setup also got no reply, so it couldn't tell when its id was free (D5). ## What, per upstream PR ### D5: `stopped` for a subscription stopped before it starts (this PR's original change) - `interop/handler/socket.ts`: `subscription.stop` goes through `stopCall`, which marks the id as stopping, interrupts the call's fiber and waits for it to end. A subscription interrupted by a stop before it sent `stopped` sends it from `Effect.onInterrupt`, once. - A closed socket, `dispose()` and `serve()` release still send nothing, so `wsLink` resends those subscriptions with their `lastEventId` after reconnecting (decision `v11-interop-handler.md`). A stop for an id with no running call is still ignored. - Where v12 still differs from v11: v11 sends `stopped` once setup settles, while v12 sends it as soon as the call is interrupted. After a stop, a procedure that rejects with an unrelated error gets `error` on v11 and `stopped` on v12; with the #7704 port below, v12's `onError` gets that error. ### #7888 (report subscription teardown errors after a stop): ported, on v12's own mechanism - #7908 (landed on `v12` while this PR was open) gave the HTTP subscription handlers `reportSubscriptionTeardown()`: a per-call `SubscriptionTeardown` service that `toEventStream` reads, so `returnUnawaited` hands what the iterator throws after the stream stopped (a pending `next()`'s rejection, a rejecting `return()`) to `onError`, and `reportTeardown` does the same for a failing Effect `Stream` finalizer. An `AbortError` isn't reported: it's how an aborted call ends. - This PR's first version added its own `CurrentLateErrors` service for the same job. Rebased onto #7908, it's dropped: the v11 interop socket and the native socket now pass `reportSubscriptionTeardown()` in a subscription call's `services`, as `server/handler/subscription.ts` and the OpenAPI handler do. One mechanism covers HTTP and sockets. - `returnUnawaited` also reports a `return()` that throws synchronously instead of rejecting; it was dropped before (own commit, with its test). - Not applicable: #7888's observable-teardown case, since v12 subscriptions have no observables. - Docs: `subscriptions/overview.md` says what reaches `onError` after a stop or close. - Regression check: on `v12` (b24a2bdf4) plus the test commit only, 6 of 18 tests fail (interop: a generator's throw after a stop and after a close, a rejecting cleanup after a stop; native: the same after an abort and a close), each with `onError` never called. With the socket handlers passing `reportSubscriptionTeardown()`, 18 of 18 pass. For the synchronous throw: without the `returnUnawaited` change, "a cleanup that throws instead of rejecting after an abort goes to onError" fails (`expected [] to deeply equal [ [ 'active', 'cleanup threw' ] ]`); with it, 8 of 8 pass. ### #7704 (subscription lifecycle): the parts v12 lacked, ported - **Late iterable disposed.** `resolve()` in `execute.ts` waits for the procedure's promise through a new `settled()` helper instead of `Effect.promise`. When the call was already interrupted, an async iterable it resolves to is disposed (`return()`, never `next()`), and what that or the rejection fails with goes to the call's `SubscriptionTeardown`, so a subscription's `onError` gets it (an `AbortError` excepted). Other calls have no reporter, and a test pins that an aborted query's late rejection reports nothing. - **Signal aborted when iteration fails.** New `InterruptSignal.abortUnlessDone(stream)`: it aborts when the stream fails or is interrupted, not when it ends. Both socket handlers wrap their subscription streams in it. `abortOnInterrupt` is unchanged, since `effects.test.ts` pins that a failed wrapped effect doesn't abort. - **Skipped: the id stays owned until cleanup settles, and the iteration error is sent after cleanup.** Both need the handler to await `return()`. That reverses `v11-stream-cancel-and-interop-parity.md` (`returnUnawaited`, so shutdown never hangs). In v12, a hung cleanup would also stall the connection's sequential frame loop, since a stop waits for the call's fiber, and `FiberMap.clear` on shutdown. In v11, it holds only that id. #7892's per-attempt ids (below) remove the id reuse that motivated it on the client side. - Regression check, late iterable: on `v12` plus the tests only (without `settled()`), 4 of 21 fail (interop: stop and close during the procedure never call `return()`; native: the same after an abort; interop: the unrelated rejection never reaches `onError`). With the fix, 21 of 21 pass. - Regression check, abort on failure: on `v12` plus the tests only, 3 of 24 fail (interop: an iteration that throws or rejects; native: a failed iteration), each timing out on a cleanup waiting for the signal. The new `effects.test.ts` test for `abortUnlessDone` fails too (4 of 42 in all). With the fix, 42 of 42 pass. ### #7889 (`wsLink` retry with the same id hangs): test ported, fix not needed - v12's `makeSocketLink` already removes a call's entry only if it still holds that call's inbox, which is the same delete-by-reference as #7889's `RequestManager` fix. - New `client/links/socket-retry.test.ts`: `retryLink` over `wsLink` against a real server retries a failed query and subscription and both settle. - Regression check: none possible, since the test passes on unmodified `v12`; it pins the behavior. ### #7892 (each `wsLink` attempt gets its own wire id): ported - `client/links/socket.ts`: a per-link counter gives each attempt, a reconnect's included, its own wire id. `Call.request` takes the id it's sent under, so a retry that reuses `op.id` no longer receives the frames still arriving for the attempt it replaced. - Regression check: with the test only, "a retry doesn't get the frames still arriving for the attempt it replaces" fails (`expected [ 1 ] to deeply equal [ 2 ]`: the retry got the stale attempt's event). With the fix, it passes. ### #7891 (`connectionParams` errors on reconnect; throwing `onClose`/`onError`): adapted - v12's socket link has no `onOpen`/`onClose`/`onError` callbacks and no connection-state observable, so the callback half doesn't apply. - The error half does: a connection that doesn't open now fails the call with `NETWORK_ERROR` "The connection could not be opened" and the error that kept it from opening as `cause`. That error is what `connectionParams` threw, or the transport's `SocketError` with the constructor's error on its open reason. Subscriptions still retry first and fail with the last attempt's error; queries and mutations fail at once, as before. The code stays `NETWORK_ERROR`, so retry and reconnect behavior is unchanged. - Docs: the Reconnects section of `client/links/ws.md`. - Regression check: on `v12` plus the new `socket-open.test.ts` only, 3 of 4 fail (`expected TrpcError: The connection was lost … to match object { code: 'NETWORK_ERROR', message: 'The connection could not be opened' }`). The 4th, a subscription that recovers after one throw, matches v11's first-connect parity test and passes on both. With the fix, 4 of 4 pass. ### #7861 (reject cross-origin WebSocket upgrades in docs and examples): ported as docs - v12 already has this in `cors()` from `@trpc12/trpc/http`: it refuses an upgrade from another origin with `403` (adapters overview), and it wraps `createV11Handler`'s upgrades through its `middleware` too. - `migrations/from-v11/serve-v11-clients.md` now says so, for v11 apps that authenticate with cookies. - New test in `interop/handler/socket.test.ts`: `cors({ allowedOrigins })` in the v11 handler's `middleware` lets an allowed origin upgrade (`101`) and refuses another (`403`). With the middleware removed, it fails (`expected 101 to be 403`). ### Not applicable to `next/` - **#7896**, **#7899** and **#7900** (connection-state callbacks and `behaviorSubject` delivery; #7899 and #7900 merged to `main` at 17:18, before this landed): v12's socket link has no connection-state observable, `onConnectionStateChange` or `behaviorSubject`, and `interop/link.ts` only adapts v11 links. The v11 code reaches `v11/` with the merges of `main`. - **#7725** (a v11 client batch that fails to send left its other requests pending): v12's socket link doesn't batch; each call sends its own request on its own fiber. A throwaway probe against a real server confirmed it: of three concurrent queries, the two whose input can't be encoded fail, the third resolves, and a later query works. - **#7833** and **#7860** (v11's `wsClient` reset its backoff when the server rejected a connection, an `id: null` error then a close, and reconnected in a tight loop; #7860 clears the rejected flag on a `result`): v12 has no rejected flag to port. It runs `createContext` per message, so a connection is never rejected as a whole. A connection-level `id: null` error (an unsupported protocol version, an invalid message) fails every call on the connection, subscriptions included, with that error, without reconnecting. A connection dropped before the server sent anything counts toward `reconnect.attempts`. Landed after this PR as 8e2db6379 (`client/links/socket-rejected.test.ts` and a paragraph in `ws.md`'s Reconnects): a subscription the server rejects fails with `UNAUTHORIZED` on one connection, and one whose oversized input the server keeps closing with 1009 (`maxPayload`) fails after its 2 reconnects. Both pass on `v12`. Each loops until it times out with the bug put back: the link ignoring the `id: null` error, or every drop counting as answered. - **#7733** (the connection state stayed `connecting` after `close()`): v12's socket link has no connection state; `close()` fails the calls in flight and leaves the link idle until the next call opens a connection (`socket-dispose.test.ts`). - **#7727** (a retired WebSocket's late `close` and `error` events disturbed the connection that replaced it): each v12 `Connection` handles only its own events. `lose(conn)` fails the calls on that connection, and `drop(conn)` invalidates the shared connection only while it's still `conn`, so a retired one closing leaves the new one alone. - **#7884** (a throwing observable teardown on abort crashed the server): v12 has no observables. Its analog, a `return()` that throws instead of rejecting after an abort, goes to `onError`; a native socket test covers it. - **#7858** (`maxBatchSize`): v12 already caps v11 WebSocket batches at `batch.maxItems` (decision `v11-interop-handler.md`; required option since #7864), and the native protocol has no array batches. ## Effect-specific choices - `settled()` in `execute.ts` waits on the procedure's promise with `Effect.callback`, so an interrupted call's late value is still observed (disposed or reported) instead of dropped, as `Effect.promise` would. - `abortUnlessDone` is `Stream.onExit`: it reads the stream's `Exit` and aborts unless it's a success, so failure and interruption share one path. - Teardown errors go to `onError` through #7908's `SubscriptionTeardown` Context service, passed in the call's `services`, not through a socket-only callback. - A connection that doesn't open keeps its typed error: `connected()` takes it from the `RcRef` acquire's `Cause` with `Cause.findErrorOption`, and the transport's `SocketError` stays the `cause`. - A stop is fiber interruption (`FiberMap.remove`); the interop handler's `stopped` reply is an `Effect.onInterrupt` finalizer, so it's sent once whichever way the call ends. ## Tests changed - This PR's own test "stop during the procedure replies stopped, which then rejects with an unrelated error" asserted that `onError` isn't called. With #7704's port, that rejection goes to `onError` (`[['pending', 'setup failed']]`); the `AbortError` case still reports nothing. No existing `v12` test was modified. - `socket-lifecycle.test.ts` passes `batch: { maxItems: 100 }`, required since #7864 landed on `v12`. ## Alternatives considered - **Await `return()` in the socket handlers**, as v11 does for #7704: set aside, see the #7704 section. - **Abort the signal on failure in `abortOnInterrupt` itself:** it's shared with HTTP calls, and a test pins that it doesn't abort when the wrapped effect fails. `abortUnlessDone` is scoped to socket subscription streams. - **Keep a socket-only late-error service** (this PR's first version, `CurrentLateErrors`): once #7908 landed, it would have been a second way to report the same failures. The sockets use #7908's `SubscriptionTeardown` instead. - **#7891: fail on a new error code, or stop retrying after a `connectionParams` error:** a new code changes the link's declared errors and `matchError()` keys; giving up early differs from v11, which keeps retrying. - **D5: send nothing (option B),** or tell a stop from a close by the interrupt cause: `FiberMap.remove` and `FiberMap.clear` both interrupt with `internalFiberId`, so a set of ids being stopped tells them apart. ## Testing From `next/`, on Node 26.12.0, rebased on `origin/v12` (b24a2bdf4, after #7905, #7906 and #7908): - `pnpm test`: 174 files, 2,011 tests pass, no type errors. - `pnpm typecheck` (59 tasks) and `pnpm check` (`vp check` and `lint:docs`) pass, and `vp check` passes on each commit's changed files at that commit. - `pnpm coverage`: 129 files and 1,407 tests pass; all thresholds met (branches 5,691 of 5,807, 98.00%; the uncovered branches in the files this PR touches are `v12`'s). Every line of the new code is covered. - `pnpm docs:build` (on 1a9dad92c; the later `v12` commits change no docs): passes, and all 698 of trpc.io's URLs work. - Flakes seen locally, neither in code this PR touches: on 5fa8c95c6, one full run timed out in `cloudflare/hibernation.test.ts` ("closing the socket stops its subscriptions", 5 s under full-suite load); it passed 5 of 5 alone, 16 of 16 with 8 copies in parallel, the full rerun, and isn't in the last 15 failed `next.yml` runs. On 1a9dad92c, one coverage run failed `packages/experimental-react/src/dom.test.tsx`'s 2 s timing test; it passed 3 of 3 alone and on the rerun. - CI was green on the two previous heads (7d7a8755d, 9871ecc49). - Landed as e2664e340 (squash of 67ab550a9; CI was green on the PR). The `next` run on `v12` for e2664e340 failed only `effect-latest`'s `experimental-react` `dom.test.tsx` "select reads cached data without suspending" (`expected [ Array(1) ] to have a length of 2 but got 1`). That's a `v12` flake from before this PR: the same assertion failed in `effect-latest` on 9f311b648 and ecc34ea9f on Nov 3, and it passes 3 of 3 locally. ## AI model Claude Opus 5.5

items.title: feat(v12): experimental path separator for RPC URLs (#5752)
items.body:
🤖 v12's counterpart of #7845, with #7845's final design, which was approved. Refs #5752. Records the answer in [`decisions/path-separator.md`](next/.agent-docs/decisions/path-separator.md) and deletes `open/path-separator.md`. ## Why - Some users sit behind firewalls or WAFs that block `.` in URL paths, so `/trpc/post.byId` never reaches the server (#5752). - Q10.2 keeps `.` as the default. This adds an opt-in that changes the URL only. ## What - `createFetchHandler({ experimental_pathSeparator: '~' })` serves `/trpc/post~byId`. The dotted URL still works, so the server can move before its clients. - `httpLink({ experimental_pathSeparator: '~' })` sends to it. Queries, mutations, SSE and byte-stream calls all use one URL builder. - `experimental_generateOpenApi(router, { target: 'rpc', experimental_pathSeparator })` documents the same URLs. Operation ids stay `post.byId`. - The type is `'.' | '_' | '~' | '-'`, checked by types only, with no runtime validation. The docs recommend `'~'`. - A router key that contains the separator is refused, because two paths would share one URL (`get_user` and `get.user` with `'_'`). The eager tree is checked when the handler is created. A lazy subtree is checked when the first URL call loads it. ```ts const handler = createFetchHandler({ router, experimental_pathSeparator: '~' }); const client = createTrpcClient({ router: routerType(), links: [httpLink({ url: '/trpc', experimental_pathSeparator: '~' })], }); // GET /trpc/post~byId?input=…; middleware still sees path 'post.byId' ``` ## Design How it follows #7845: - **Allowed characters.** `'.' | '_' | '~' | '-'` are the punctuation characters in RFC 3986's "unreserved" set. URLs never escape them, normalizers leave them alone, and routes give them no meaning. `/` is left out because it needs catch-all routes in every adapter and framework, and URL parsing rewrites `..` and `//`. - **No runtime check.** The first draft's regex check is gone. - **Default resolved once.** The `'.'` default is applied where the public options are read: `makeHttpHandler`, `makeTransport` and `generateDocument`. Internal helpers (`makeUrlPaths`, `toUrlPath`) take a concrete `PathSeparator`. - **Router-key check kept.** Same behaviour as before. Where it differs from #7845: - **Placement.** The option is on the handler and the link, not on `initTrpc`. v12 already puts what shapes the wire there (`endpoint`, `batch`, and the serializer since Q11.5). - **Name.** It keeps the `experimental_` prefix. URL-only mapping is safe for the same reasons as before. Router keys can't contain `.`, so a dotted path and a tuple hold the same information. The URL is the only thing a firewall sees. TanStack Query keys are already tuples and don't change. The full audit, and why tuple paths on the client weren't taken, are in the decision record. ## Testing - `packages/trpc/src/server/handler/path-separator.test.ts` covers: - end-to-end calls with `'~'`: query, mutation, SSE and a lazy subtree, with exact URL paths; - dotted paths in middleware and `createContext`, and each of `'_'`, `'~'` and `'-'`; - batching, the dotted URL still being served, and a client/handler mismatch giving `NOT_FOUND`; - eager and lazy key clashes, and the RPC OpenAPI document; - type tests: the option is exactly `'.' | '_' | '~' | '-'`, and `'/'` and `','` don't compile. - Passing locally: `pnpm check`, `pnpm typecheck` (59 tasks), `pnpm test` (164 files, 1868 tests), `pnpm docs:build` and `pnpm --filter www decisions:check`. - The `branch-name` CI job fails because the branch is `cursor/…`. That's expected: the cleanup of that rule is a separate pending decision.
